BACKGROUND OF THE PARTIES
The California State University (hereafter "the University" or "the CSU" or “Management”)
provides higher education to approximately 417,000 students across twenty-three campuses and
employs approximately 25,500 faculty and over 26,500 support staff employees. It is the
nation's largest university and offers courses in a wide range of disciplines. The University is
publicly supported and receives financial support from the State of California through the
appropriation process. The system is led by a Chancellor appointed by a governing body of
twenty-five members of the Board of Trustees.
The Teamsters Local 2010 (hereafter “Teamsters” or “Union”) has represented approximately
1100 workers of Unit 6 (Skilled Trades) at 22 of the 23 campuses and Chancellor’s office since
2017. The “Skilled Trades” consists of employees such as carpenters, electricians, plumbers,
locksmiths, painters, mechanics, masons, metal workers, building services engineers,
refrigeration mechanics, power plant operators, general facilities workers and related
occupations, including apprentices.
The parties ratified a Collective Bargaining Agreement effective March 2024 through June 2026.
STATEMENT OF ISSUES BEFORE THE FACTFINDING PANEL
The impasse has to do with one item of the Collective Bargaining Agreement (“CBA”), Article
24: SALARY, specifically 24.7:
“Step Progression is the movement from an employee’s current salary step to a higher salary step.
Eligibility criteria for step advancement will be subject to negotiations in successor bargaining.
a. For fiscal year 2025/2026, effective July 1, 2025 there will be one Step Progression for all
employees (except those at or above the top step of their classification).
In addition, for employees who are below their Target Step as of July 1, 2025 they will be placed
at their Target Step.
The Step Progression in 24.7a will not occur unless and until the contingency below is met.
This Step Progression is contingent upon the State of California’s final Budget Act of 2025
containing a new, unallocated, ongoing appropriation to the CSU not less than $480 million
above the final Budget Act of 2023. The $480 million represents the 2024-2025 and the 2025-
2026 CSU compact funding commitment. The final Budget Act of 2025 has an expected
enactment date between June 27, 2025, and October 15, 2025.
If the above contingency is not met then the Union and CSU shall re-open negotiations on Article
24 (Salary) and Article 25 (Benefits).” Underlined for emphasis by the Chair.

FACTFINDING CRITERIA
This factfinding is governed by the provisions of the Higher Education Employer-Employee
Relations Act (HEERA), which unlike the other public employment statutes, does not
provide specific criteria to be considered by factfinders, except that the factfinding panel’s
recommendations shall be advisory. In developing advisory recommendations, the criteria
set forth in the Education Employment Relations Act (EERA) can be helpful in determining
how the factfinders should consider, weigh, and be guided by the evidence and testimony
provided by the parties:
1. State and federal laws that are applicable to the Employer.
2. Stipulations of the parties.
3. The interests and welfare of the public and the financial ability of the public
schools.
4. Comparison of the wages, hours, and conditions of employment of the employees
involved in the fact-finding proceeding with the wages, hours, and conditions of
employment of other employees performing similar services and with other
employees generally in public school employment in comparable communities.
5. The Consumer Price Index for goods and services, commonly known as the cost of
living.
6. The overall compensation presently received by the employees, including direct
wage compensation, vacations, holidays, and other excused time, insurance and
pensions, medical and hospitalization benefits, the continuity and stability of
employment, and all other benefits received.
7. Such other facts not confined to those specified in paragraphs 1 through 6,
inclusive, which are normally and traditionally taken into consideration in making
such findings and recommendations.
HISTORY OF NEGOTIATIONS
In the CBA ratified in 2024, the parties agreed upon a new salary structure involving “Steps” and
“Step Progression”, which was a phased-in method to move the unit members into a new
schedule. From the materials presented, the Chair recognizes the efforts of the parties to reach
this long-sought interest on behalf of the workers. The new pay system or schedule was agreed
to be phased in over the term of the Agreement and used the Governor’s Higher Education
Compact as the basis for the agreement. This Higher Education Compact was a five year
agreement with the Governor promising new, ongoing, 5% annual base funding through fiscal
year 2026/27.
The Budget Act of 2025, which provided the final budget for the State, which provided the final
budget for the State, cut $143.8 from the base. Management then invoked the contingency
clause of 24.7 for the 2025/26 contract year. The Union disagreed with this interpretation and
filed a grievance and an Unfair Labor Practice Charge with the Public Employment Relations
Board.

The Parties met for a bargaining session on October 23, 2025 and after an exchange of proposals,
declared impasse. A mediation session on December 12, 2025 was also unsuccessful and the
mediator certified the parties to Factfinding, under HEERA.

Chair’s Recommendations
The parties entered into agreement for the 2025/26 Salary adjustments, which were a mutual
priority for both sides. The negotiators obviously thought the new system and schedule to be
reasonable and affordable IF the promised funding was not cut. But it was. It is clear to the
Chair that the University can afford to implement the agreed-upon provisions for a unit of this
size, even taking in the consideration of the cut with the interest-free loan from the state. The
Governor’s proposed budget for 2026/27 is positive for funding the 5 year “Compact” with
Higher Education in the State, with a proposed deferral of the interest-free loan for this year.
With that proposed budget in mind, the Chair recommends the following:

The neutral fact-finding Chair’s report correctly and thoughtfully analyzes the central question
presented in this impasse: whether the University received the funding necessary to implement
the 2025/26 salary increases contemplated under the parties’ agreement. The University
appreciates the Chair’s clear and unambiguous finding that the CSU did not receive the
additional funding required to trigger the increases.
That conclusion is consistent with the plain language of the agreement and the undisputed
budgetary facts. The facts are clear: the State reduced CSU’s base appropriation by $143.8
million, and while the University subsequently secured a one-year, zero-interest loan to mitigate
that reduction, no new ongoing funds were provided in 2025/26. The contractual contingency was
therefore not satisfied, as CSU has consistently maintained, and as the Chair found.
CSU cannot responsibly implement ongoing salary increases based on the Governor’s proposed
2026/27 budget. A proposed budget is not an enacted budget, and proposed funding does not
constitute guaranteed funding. For that exact reason, the parties negotiated clear contingent
language tying the 2025/26 salary adjustments to receipt of specified funding. Implementing
ongoing increases absent that specified funding would effectively convert a negotiated
contingency into a guaranteed obligation.
The Governor’s January proposal reflects an intent to continue Compact funding, but that
proposal is dependent on revenue projections that remain uncertain until the legislative adoption.
In fact, the Legislative Analyst’s Office has projected a more cautious revenue outlook than that
reflected in the Governor’s proposal. If the Governor’s proposed funding is enacted, the Chair's
proposal would merit consideration. However, until funding is enacted on a continuing basis, it
would be fiscally irresponsible for CSU to create permanent salary obligations.
CSU must administer compensation consistently across its 14 bargaining units representing
approximately 70,000 employees. The University has a longstanding practice of treating
represented employee groups similarly with respect to general salary increases. Implementing an
ongoing increase for one bargaining unit — even one of relatively small size — will create a

across the system would result in nearly $300 million in permanent annual costs for which no
guaranteed funding currently exists. CSU cannot responsibly undertake such a structural
obligation absent reliable, ongoing state support.
For these reasons, the University values the Chair’s careful consideration and appreciates the
critical findings regarding the absence of additional funding. However, CSU cannot agree to
implement ongoing salary increases without a secured and ongoing appropriations reflected in
an enacted State budget sufficient to sustain them. CSU remains committed to bargaining in good
faith and to revisiting salary adjustments once reliable, ongoing funding is approved and
materialized.

TEAMSTERS LOCAL 2010'S PARTIAL CONCURRENCE AND PARTIAL DISSENT
TO THE FACTFINDING RECOMMENDATIONS
PERB CASE NO. LA-IM-4203-H
I. INTRODUCTION
Teamsters Local 20 IO concurs with the Factfinder·s determination that the University has
the ability to pay the July 2025 contractual wage increases and his recommendation that those
wage increases should be implemented. Teamsters Local 2010 further concurs with the
Factfinder's report in that it did not find any of the statutory factfinding criteria to support the
University's position. Teamsters Local 20 IO dissents from the Factfinder's recommendation that
that the increases be implemented January 2026 rather than July 2025 as provided in the contract.
As the Factfinder's report notes, the 2024-2026 CBA between Teamsters Local 20 IO and
the California State University (University) created a new salary structure with steps and an annual
step progression in addition to across-the-board cost-of-living increases for the Unit 6 (Skilled
Trades) employees. The parties· CBA provides that effective July I, 2025, Unit 6 employees
receive a I% cost-of-living increase, progress one step on the structure, and that the thirteen
percent of Unit 6 employees still below their ··target step·· based on years of service would be
brought up. The University reopened the contract on wages and has insisted to impasse on its
proposal that Unit 6 forego its base-building wage increases and take a one-time lump sum
payment of 3% instead. Teamsters Local 20 IO has proposed that the University pay the contractual
wage increases, retroactive to July 2025, plus penalties and interest.
II. TEAMSTERS LOCAL 2010 CONCURS THAT THE UNIVERSITY HAS THE
ABILITY TO PAY THE CONTRACTUAL WAGE INCREASES
Teamsters Local 2010 concurs in the Factfinder's determination that the University can
afford to implement the agreed-upon wage increases set forth in the CBA. Teamsters Local 20 I 0
further concurs with the Factfinder's determination that the Governor's proposed budget for
2026/27 reflects the State's plan to restore all funding to the University and the University is slated
to receive a 7% base increase. These findings establish that third factfinding criterion (the
University's ability to pay) favors Teamsters Local 2010's position that the University should pay
the negotiated and promised wage increases.
In addition to the ability to pay, the other factfinding criteria support Teamsters Local
20 I O's position.

III. THE CONSUMER PRICE INDEX SUPPORTS THE UNION'S PROPOSAL
The fifth factfinding criterion (the Consumer Price Index) for goods and services supports
Teamsters Local 2010's proposal. CPI is 3.2%. The University's proposal to eliminate the 2026/27
salary increases (and pay a one-time lump sum equal to 3%) amounts to a cut in Unit 6 worker's
real take home pay. This evidence was undisputed by the University.
IV. COMPARISON WITH EMPLOYEES PERFORMING SIMILAR SERVICES IN
COMPARABLE COMMUNITIES SUPPORTS THE UNION'S PROPOSAL
The fou1th factfinding criterion (comparators) supports Teamsters Local 2010's proposal.
No other California public university or county has imposed wage freezes on its employees in
2025/26. The UCs have provided 4% and 5% to its skilled trades employees. California's
significant cities and counties have provided 3-7% increases.
The contractual 2025/26 wage increases were pa1t of the agreement to attempt to remedy
the wage stagnation and lack of comparability for CSU skilled trades works. Unit 6 employees had
stagnated in compensation with the University's lack of a step structure resulting in 82% of the
unit below the median salary range and lagging 28.6% behind comparable UC campuses in the
same counties as CSU employees. The negotiated wage increases were important to the University
making progress on closing these gaps. However, these comparators are receiving additional wage
increases in 2025/26. Thus, the University is now falling farther behind.
Finally, the University's failure to follow through on its promise has left the employees
receiving the lowest wages relative to years of service the worst off. There are no comparators
where employees with long tenure are treated worse with respect to wages and compensation.
V. TEAMSTERS LOCAL 2010'S PARTIALLY CONCURS AND PARTIALLY
DISSENTS TO THE CHAIR'S RECOMMENDED PROPOSAL
Teamsters Local 2010 concurs with the Factfinder that the 2025/26 wage increases should
be put into effect. Teamsters Local 20 IO dissents from the recommendation to delay the
implementation to January I, 2026. Given the Factfinder's correct determination that the
University can afford to implement the increases, and that all of the statutory factfinding criteria
support it, the University must implement the contractual promise to implement the 2025/26 wage
increases effective July I, 2025.
